car.why: Car pace: characteristics blended into one score with weights from the track profile (aero tracks reward downforce, power tracks reward power and low drag). Each point above the reference score is 0.17% of lap time, so a 15-point gap between front and back of the grid gives the plan's 2–3%.

weightSPerKgPer90s.why: Seconds per kg per lap, scaled to a 90 s lap: 10 kg of excess weight or fuel costs ~0.3 s (plan 5.4).

driver.why: Driver pace: each point of pace above 88 is 0.045% of lap time, so the grid's 16-point spread is ~0.7% — smaller than the car spread, as in real F1. Form and morale around 70 nudge it; wet skill matters only on a wet track, up to 1.2% per 10 points at full wetness.

lapNoiseSd.why: Lap-to-lap scatter (seconds, sd), interpolated by the consistency attribute: grid drivers at 78–94 land in the plan's 0.2–0.4 s band.

fatigue.why: Fatigue 0..100 builds each lap, faster in heat and on high-g tracks, slower with stamina. Above 30 it costs 0.05 s/lap and +12% mistake chance per 10 points — a tired driver fades and errs late in a hot race (plan 5.16).

mistakes.why: Driver errors: ~0.4% per lap for a consistency-85 driver, far likelier in the wet and on the wrong tyre. Most are small moments; one in six is a spin, and one spin in seven ends in the barrier. Even the most consistent driver keeps a 0.05% chance per lap. How often a spin ends in the barrier scales with the track: ×(0.4 + 1.2 × SC profile), so walls close by (street circuits) turn errors into crashes and run-off forgives them.

start.why: Standing start: grid slots 0.2 s apart, and an even slot — the dirty side, off the racing line — costs another 0.07 s off the line (plan 5.3). 2.2 s lost accelerating from rest; the starts attribute gains or loses 0.02 s per point with 0.3 s of random spread, and one car in forty bogs down, losing 0.6–1.8 s (three to nine places). The launch sets the order into the first corner: a car that gets away better than the one in front is ahead of it without an overtaking move; each car has a 1.2% chance of lap-1 contact.

traffic.why: A car cannot run closer than 0.3 s without passing. Within 1.5 s it loses up to 0.15 s per sector in dirty air, scaled by the track aero sensitivity and by the car: each point of dirty-air tolerance above 80 cuts the loss by 2%. Within 1 s the tow gives back up to 0.08 s per sector on straights. Lapping costs the backmarker 0.35 s and the leader 0.1 s. The aero-sensitivity scaling is (0.5 + sensitivity), so even a power track costs some time in the wake.

drs.why: DRS: ~0.3 s over a zone 12% of the lap long (scaled by the actual zone), for a car within 1 s at detection; enabled from lap 3 and off for two laps after a restart.

overtaking.why: Overtake probability is a logistic function: the attacker's pace advantage over a lap in seconds, measured in clean air from each car's remembered sector pace (a new lap weighs 0.4 of it, so one scruffy lap does not decide a duel) (this sector as driven now, the other two as last driven — a car faster all round gets a better run at the passing place), DRS, the racecraft gap, the tyre-wear gap and an ERS push raise it; a hard track to pass (overtakingDifficulty) and passing outside a DRS zone lower it. Failed attempts cost both cars time; about one attack in a hundred ends in contact for a normal driver (twice that for an aggressive one, half for a calm one — see radio) — attacks are real lunges now that hopeless ones are not made, so each carries the risk the many half-attempts of M2 used to share (it keeps collision safety cars, and so SC in ~40% of races). The pace advantage counts only up to 1.15 s a lap: a car that has run wide is not automatically passable on a narrow street circuit. A spun car is driven around, not overtaken. Away from a DRS zone a car only attempts when at least 0.25 s faster over the sector. A driver only lunges when the chance is at least 5%: below that he follows and keeps the ERS charge, instead of wasting it and 0.25 s on a move that is not on. The chance rises steeply with the pace advantage and the track's difficulty weighs less than in M2: the chance rises steeply with it: at a hard track (difficulty 0.7) with DRS an attack from 0.3 s a lap faster comes off about once in eighty, from 1 s faster about once in four (with two DRS zones, a pass within a lap or two); at Monaco even 1 s a lap buys only one in seven; the calendar averages ~40 overtakes and Monaco ~10. A repelled attack is reported once per duel, again only after 10 laps: duels are common (~45 a race) and the feed must stay readable.

ers.why: ERS battery 0..1: recharges 0.35 per lap and an attack or a defence costs half a charge, so a car can push roughly every other lap. The system quality itself already counts in car pace (car.powerMix.ers); here it scales how much a push is worth relative to the reference deployment of 84.

fuel.why: Fuel use per lap is the track's figure, 0.4% lower per point of fuel efficiency above 83; cars fuel exactly to the flag plus a 1.5 kg margin, and one standard deviation of whatever the team is unsure about on top — not knowing your own consumption is carried as weight.

pit.why: Pit stop = the track's pit-lane loss + a stationary time of ~2.5 s, 0.02 s better per point of crew quality above 80, with 0.2 s scatter and a 3% chance of a sticky wheel nut (+2–8 s). Under a safety car the whole stop costs 55% of normal, under a VSC 70%. No stop is quicker than 1.8 s stationary. A team without a chief mechanic counts as a 40-rated crew lead.

reliability.why: Mechanical failures per race = 0.45 × (1 − reliability): a 0.85-reliability car fails ~7% of races, close to real modern DNF rates. A third of failures are partial (0.9 s/lap slower to the flag); 60% come from the power unit.

damage.why: Contact: usually front-wing damage worth 0.8 s/lap until the next stop; a third of contacts puncture a tyre, one in five ends the race.

stewards.why: Contact in a fight is looked at by the stewards, and about one in three is judged the attacker's fault: five seconds added at the flag (plan 5.3). Enough to cost a place in a close finish, not enough to end a race.

sprint.why: A sprint runs a third of the race distance (plan 5.3, раздел 10 п. 4): long enough for tyres to matter, short enough that nobody needs to stop.

raceControl.why: Race control: a crash brings the safety car 10% + 90% × the track SC profile of the time, otherwise a VSC; a stranded car is usually handled with a VSC (12% + 30% × profile), sometimes the safety car; debris from contact sometimes a safety car. Background incidents (debris, stray objects) add ~0.5 × profile triggers per race. Race control needs 6-16 s to see an incident, decide and show the flag, so the field keeps racing towards it meanwhile. SC laps run 40% slower and the field closes to 0.8 s gaps; a VSC slows everyone equally. Calibrated so a track SC profile is roughly its share of races with a safety car, and the calendar averages ~40% (docs/calibration/M2.md). Behind the safety car or under VSC tyres wear at 40% and fuel burns at 60% of the racing rate. A car more than 1.5 bunch gaps behind the car ahead drives faster than safety-car pace to close up.

strategy.why: Strategist decisions: a plan 30 s slower than the best (a pit call 20 s worse) scores zero, so perception noise from decide.json means ~0.75 s of misjudgement for a top strategist and ~7 s for a poor one. Plans have up to 2 stops (3-stoppers are rarely right in the modern era; pit calls can still add a stop). A risk-loving strategist gets 0.02 per stop saved per unit of risk above 0.5, tipping near-equal plans towards fewer stops. Wetness moving by 0.08 triggers a tyre review; a safety car within 12 laps of a planned stop triggers a pit call. No planned stint is shorter than 5 laps. Below wetness 0.1 only slicks are considered; otherwise any compound within 6 s a lap of the best one for the conditions. Each stop also costs track position the car has to win back on the road: 15 s × the track overtaking difficulty — ~15 s where passing is nearly impossible, ~4 s where it is easy — so strategists stop less where they cannot pass. The goal the player sets tips plans and pit calls by 0.02 per stop: towards fewer stops to keep a place, more to go after places. The pit window is every lap where stopping costs at most 2 s more than the best lap to stop. The finish forecast is ±0.5 place at the flag and ±3 at the start (0.5 + 2.5 × the share of the race still to run), wider for a weak strategist (×1.8) and narrower for a strong one (×0.8); rival pace is read from their last 3 laps. Each rival counts as ahead with a logistic chance of the projected time gap over 1.5 s + 0.1 s per lap still to run, so the forecast position moves smoothly as gaps open and close.

radio.why: Race radio (plan 5.4). Pace: push is 0.2 s a lap quicker but wears tyres 30% faster, burns 6% more fuel and makes 30% more mistakes; saving tyres costs 0.35 s and wears 30% less; lift-and-coast costs 0.5 s and saves 12% fuel. ERS attack deploys for 0.12 s a lap and drains a quarter of the battery a lap; harvesting costs 0.15 s and charges a fifth. Aggression shifts the pass odds (logit ±0.5 for the attacker, ±0.3–0.4 against the defender) and makes contact twice as likely when aggressive, half when calm. An engineer calls a battle inside 1 s and harvests below a 30% battery; a team character's risk below 0.35 means a calm driver, above 0.65 an aggressive one. A car fuelled to the flag drops to lift-and-coast when it is 0.5 kg short of what the laps left need. Engineer choices are scored on a 5 s scale of stint time, with a 0.05 nudge towards pushing in a fight and towards the mode the player asked the engineer to save.

teamOrders.why: Team orders: a swap happens when the teammate is within 1.5 s, costing both 0.4 s. Whether a driver obeys is a logistic chance: 2 (≈88%) at loyalty, ego and morale of 50, +0.03 per point of loyalty and +0.02 per point of morale above 50, −0.04 per point of ego; −1.2 when asked to yield while faster over the lap, −0.8 when yielding costs a podium or points.

segments.why: How a lap is cut into simulation segments (docs/systems/lap-segments.md). Boundaries are the three timing lines, the edges of every DRS zone and the braking point of every corner that follows a straight of at least 250 m — the places where a lap is actually decided. A segment shorter than 4% of the lap is merged away, and anything longer than 12% is split evenly, so no stretch runs unwatched for more than an eighth of a lap and every track lands between 9 and 14 segments rather than at a hundred or at three.

motion.why: How the track map moves a car inside a sector — drawing only, the race's timing lines are untouched. The track is sampled every 5 m; the corner radius over ±20 m caps the speed at √(35 m/s² × R) (about 3.6 g: ~90 km/h at a 20 m hairpin, ~250 km/h at 140 m); cars accelerate at 11 m/s² and brake at 45 m/s² (about 4.6 g) between corners, up to 330 km/h. Only the shape counts: the replay spreads each sector's real time along it, so a car brakes into corners and runs fast on straights.
